text: A single commercial threat feed can publish tens of thousands of IOCs a day, and most of them have nothing to do with you. If every one of those gets written straight into a detection rule or a high-priority watchlist, analysts learn within a week that alerts tied to threat intel are usually noise — and they start ignoring them, which is the exact failure this lesson is built to prevent.

The fix is combining three signals instead of trusting any single one. Confidence is the feed's own stated certainty that an indicator is actually malicious. Relevance is whether it has anything to do with your environment at all — your tech stack, your geography, and most importantly whether Lesson 14's SIEM lookup actually saw it touch your logs. Recency is how long ago it was last reported, since a command-and-control IP from a campaign that ended over a year ago is far less actionable than one updated yesterday.

Those three signals combine into one weighted priority score. This lesson's example leans harder on confidence and relevance than on recency, because an IOC already confirmed inside your own environment is worth acting on even if the feed entry itself is a few weeks old — and that weighting is a deliberate team decision, not something to inherit by accident.

A bare number still isn't actionable on its own, so it gets mapped into tiers: eighty and above auto-promotes toward Lesson 16's detection push, fifty and above goes to an analyst review queue, everything else gets archived without action. Sorting the list before tiering also lets you cap it outright — only the top two hundred scored IOCs today — as a blunt but effective control when a feed has an unusually heavy day.

Those eighty and fifty cutoffs are a starting point, not a law of nature. The only real way to know if they're right is tracking what happens after a human reviews the analyst-review tier, and whether auto-promoted IOCs are routinely correct — and tuning the thresholds from that feedback before any of this intel is trusted to reach a live detection rule, which is exactly where the next lesson picks up.
